en: Cariyāpiṭaka, Hatthināgavagga, Sīlapāramī 7: The Perfection of Virtue of the Elephant King Mahāpaduma. Once upon a time, O monks, the Bodhisatta was born as the elephant king Mahāpaduma in the Himalayas. He was seven cubits high and possessed great strength. His body was white as a conch shell, his trunk was like a lotus stalk, and his tail was like a lotus fiber. His ears were like two outspread wings, his tusks were like two polished silver pillars, and his trunk was like a golden pillar. His face was like a full moon, and he was adorned with all the marks of a noble elephant. Now, at that time, there was a certain man who lived near the Himalayas. He was poor and destitute, and he had no means of livelihood. One day, while wandering about, he saw the elephant king Mahāpaduma. Seeing him, he thought: "This elephant is of great power and beauty; if I could but capture him, I would become wealthy and famous. With this thought in mind, he went to the king and reported the matter. The king, being pleased, gave him a large sum of money and sent him forth with a great army to capture the elephant. The man, accompanied by his troops, went to the foot of the Himalayas and set up a trap. He constructed a large pit, covered it with branches and leaves, and concealed it with grass and soil. When the elephant king Mahāpaduma came down from the mountain to drink water, he stepped into the trap. The earth beneath him gave way, and he fell into the pit. The men, seeing him fallen, bound him with strong ropes and led him away to the king. The king was greatly delighted and said: "This elephant is of great power and beauty; let him be well cared for and provided with all luxuries. And so, the elephant was given every comfort and treated with great honor. However, the man who had captured him became envious of the elephant’s prosperity. He thought: "If only this elephant would die, I would gain even greater wealth and status. With this wicked thought, he approached the elephant one day when he was alone and whispered a spell into his ear, intending to kill him. The elephant, perceiving the man's evil intent, reflected: "This man has no other purpose than to harm me. If I were to strike him back, I would be guilty of violence. It is better for me to endure this suffering and maintain my virtue. With this thought, he remained patient and did not harm the man. The man, seeing the elephant’s forbearance, was filled with remorse and wept bitterly. He confessed his sin and begged forgiveness. The elephant, moved by compassion, spoke these verses: "O man, do not fear; I have no ill will toward you. I have endured this suffering for the sake of my virtue. Patience is the highest austerity; patience is the supreme sacrifice. He who is patient and self-controlled conquers everything. Having spoken thus, the elephant king Mahāpaduma exhorted the man to abandon his evil ways and live a life of virtue. The man, having received this teaching, took refuge in the Triple Gem and practiced the precepts. Thus, O monks, the Bodhisatta, even in the form of an animal, was firm in his virtue and showed great compassion. This, monks, is called the Perfection of Virtue of the Elephant King Mahāpaduma.
The Mātaṅga Deed:
“Furthermore, when I was a matted-hair ascetic practicing fierce austerities;”
Named Mātaṅga by name,
virtuous and well-composed;
I am a brahmin alone.
We both dwell on the banks of the Ganges;
I live on the upper bank,
while the brahmin lives below.
While wandering along a favorable path,
I saw a horse above me;
having reviled me there, he—
Even if my head were to split asunder, if I were to become angry here,
I would not be guarding my virtue.
Having observed him,
I would have treated him like ashes—
him who then uttered that curse against me.
Enraged and with a wicked mind,
he fell upon his very head;
I liberated him through my meditative power.
I protected my virtue,
I did not protect my life;
for at that time, I was indeed possessed of virtue.
“Solely for the sake of awakening.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Mātaṅga Deed.
